parts.label: (a)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Start by tracing the signal path - where does a small part of the output voltage go back to in a feedback loop?
Hint 2: Think about which op-amp input it returns to and whether it adds to or opposes the original input signal.
parts.proper_answer: A fraction of the output voltage is fed back to the input and subtracted from the input voltage.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Picture the Loop**
Think of feedback as sampling. You take a small fraction of what comes out of the amplifier and feed it back round to the front again to control what happens next.

Step 2: **Why It Is Negative**
In negative feedback that sampled signal is returned to the inverting (-) input, so it is subtracted from the input signal. That is: $$V_{result} = V_{IN} - V_{feedback}$$ This opposition is what stabilises the amplifier.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Recall that an op-amp without feedback has huge open-loop gain - what must happen to that gain when you oppose the input?
Hint 2: Think about the trade-off - if gain goes down, what useful property of frequency response goes up to keep gain x bandwidth constant?
parts.proper_answer: 1. Voltage gain is reduced / stabilised. 2. Bandwidth is increased, with gain x bandwidth remaining constant.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Gain Goes Down But Becomes Stable**
Because you are constantly subtracting, the overall closed-loop gain is much smaller than the huge open-loop gain. The benefit is that the gain no longer depends on the unpredictable op-amp itself, only on the external resistors, so it is stable and predictable.

Step 2: **Bandwidth Goes Up**
There is a trade-off that helps you. For an op-amp: $$\text{gain} \times \text{bandwidth} = \text{constant}$$ So when negative feedback reduces gain, bandwidth increases. Distortion and noise are also reduced.

parts.label: (b)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Look at Fig. 8.1 - the input goes through the 800 ohm resistor to the - input with the + input earthed. Which standard op-amp configuration is this?
Hint 2: Recall how closed-loop gain depends on the ratio of the feedback resistor to the input resistor, including the sign for inversion.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Spot the Inverting Amplifier**
The non-inverting (+) input is connected to 0 V earth, and the signal goes to the inverting (-) input via the 800 ohm resistor. The 9600 ohm resistor is the feedback resistor $R_F$. This is the classic inverting amplifier.

Step 2: **Apply the Gain Formula**
For an ideal inverting amplifier: $$G = \frac{V_{OUT}}{V_{IN}} = -\frac{R_F}{R_{IN}}$$ Put in the values: $$G = -\frac{9600}{800} = -12$$ The minus sign simply means the output is inverted relative to the input.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Use your gain from (b)(i) with $V_{OUT} = G \times V_{IN}$ to calculate the ideal output for each input first.
Hint 2: Check each ideal result against the +6 V and -6 V supply rails - can the output ever go beyond the supplies?
parts.proper_answer: 1. $V_{OUT} = 1.2\text{ V}$. 2. Ideal is $-15.6\text{ V}$ so op-amp saturates, $V_{OUT} = -6\text{ V}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Multiply by Gain**
Use $$V_{OUT} = G \times V_{IN}$$ with $G = -12$. For $V_{IN} = -0.10\text{ V}$: $$V_{OUT} = (-12) \times (-0.10) = +1.2\text{ V}$$ This is inside the +6 V to -6 V supplies, so the op-amp behaves linearly and the output is $1.2\text{ V}$.

Step 2: **Spot Saturation**
For $V_{IN} = +1.3\text{ V}$: $$V_{OUT(ideal)} = (-12) \times (+1.3) = -15.6\text{ V}$$ An ideal op-amp cannot output more than its supply voltage. Since -15.6 V is more negative than the -6 V rail, the output saturates at approximately $$V_{OUT} = -6\text{ V}$$

parts.label: (b)(iii)
hints: Hint 1: Since magnitude of gain is $R_F/R_{IN}$, think which resistor you could replace with a light-sensitive component so that more light gives a smaller ratio.
parts.proper_answer: Replace the $9600\,\Omega$ feedback resistor with an LDR.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Make Gain Depend on Light**
Magnitude of gain is: $$|G| = \frac{R_F}{R_{IN}}$$ An LDR has resistance that falls as light intensity rises. If the feedback resistor $R_F$ is an LDR, then brighter light gives smaller $R_F$ and so smaller $|G|$. That gives exactly the required behaviour: magnitude of gain decreases as light intensity increases.
